notes.meaning: God gave this message to Ezekiel in the tenth year of King Jehoiachin's exile in Babylon. At that exact time, the Babylonian army was besieging Jerusalem, and the Jewish king was hoping Egypt would come and rescue them. God spoke now to show that Egypt could never save them.

The Lord told Ezekiel to turn toward Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, and speak against him and his entire country. The reigning ruler was Pharaoh Hophra, who had won many battles and felt completely safe on his throne. God wanted His people to understand that even the most powerful kings on earth answer to Him.

God described Pharaoh as a giant water creature, like a crocodile, resting proudly among the canals of the Nile River. Pharaoh bragged that the great river belonged to him and that he made it for himself. By taking credit for what God created, the king acted as if he were a god himself.

The Lord announced that He would drag Pharaoh out of his safe waters like a hunter catching a crocodile with large hooks. All the fish in the streams, representing the Egyptian soldiers and people who followed him, would cling to his scales and be pulled out too. Those who put their trust in proud leaders share in their downfall.

God promised to fling Pharaoh and his forces into the dry desert, where a water creature cannot live. Instead of receiving the grand burial that Egyptian kings cared so much about, their bodies would be left in the open field for wild animals and birds to eat. This showed how completely their human pride would be stripped away.

Through this judgment, the Egyptians would learn that the Lord alone is God. Pharaoh had offered help to the people of Israel, but he proved to be like a fragile reed growing along the Nile riverbank. When someone tries to use a hollow reed as a walking stick, it snaps under any real weight.

When Israel tried to lean on Egypt for military support, the reed splintered and tore their hands and shoulders. Egypt broke completely, leaving Israel shaken and defenseless before the Babylonian army. Leaning on human promises instead of God only brings pain and disappointment.

Because Egypt had proved faithless and deceitful, God declared that He would bring an invading army against them like a sharp sword. This warfare, along with civil strife inside the nation, would strike down both people and livestock. God's judgment would reach every part of Egyptian society.

The fertile land of Egypt would become an empty ruin so that its people would recognize the Lord's power. God repeated Pharaoh's boastful claim that he owned and created the Nile to show the exact reason for this disaster. God will not share His glory with anyone who claims to be the creator of their own success.

The Lord declared Himself the enemy of Egypt and the very waters Pharaoh boasted about. The destruction would stretch across the entire nation, from Migdol in the far north to Syene at the southern border next to Cush, or modern Ethiopia. No corner of the kingdom would escape God's reach.

God warned that Egypt would become so empty and broken that neither people nor livestock would travel through it for forty years. This set time mirrored the long years of hardship Israel had once faced in the wilderness. The proud nation would experience total helplessness under God's hand.

differ.view: The forty years is a symbolic number representing a fixed time of divine discipline and political weakness, rather than an exact historical count.
The forty years should be taken literally as an actual period of historical desolation, even if secular Egyptian records do not record it.

notes.meaning: Egypt's grand cities would lie in ruins among other ruined lands during these forty years of judgment. The Lord would also scatter the Egyptian people into foreign nations, breaking their imperial strength. The nation that once held others as slaves would now taste exile for itself.

After the forty years were over, the Lord promised to show mercy and bring the scattered Egyptians back from the lands where they had been exiled. Even when God judges proud nations, His anger does not last forever. This is a rare Old Testament promise of return given to a foreign world empire.

God promised to bring the captives back to Pathros, the southern region of Upper Egypt where their civilization first began. Yet Egypt would never return to its former glory; it would remain a lowly, dependent kingdom. God humbled them to keep them from ever dominating the ancient world again.

The Lord declared that Egypt would stay the lowest of the kingdoms and never again rise above the other nations. History shows this came true, as foreign powers like the Persians, Greeks, and Romans ruled over Egypt for centuries. God keeps proud empires from rising beyond the boundaries He sets.

A weakened Egypt would no longer tempt Israel to rely on foreign armies instead of trusting God. Looking to Egypt had only reminded God of Israel's unfaithfulness and brought punishment upon them. By removing the false crutch Israel leaned on, God helped His people look to Him alone.

Nearly seventeen years later, in the twenty-seventh year of exile, God spoke to Ezekiel again. This is the latest dated prophecy in the entire book. It is placed here so that all the messages about Egypt's future can be read together.

The Lord noted that King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon had spent thirteen hard years besieging the island city of Tyre. His soldiers rubbed their heads bald wearing heavy helmets and scraped their shoulders raw carrying heavy stones for the siege works. Yet the Tyrians loaded their treasures onto ships and escaped, leaving the army with no plunder to pay for their hard labor.

Because Nebuchadnezzar received nothing from Tyre, God announced that He would hand Egypt over to the Babylonian king. Nebuchadnezzar would easily conquer Egypt, plunder its great riches, and take its captives. This wealth would serve as the rightful payment for the Babylonian troops.

God explained that He was rewarding Nebuchadnezzar because the Babylonian army was unknowingly carrying out God's judgment against Tyre. Even pagan kings with selfish ambitions are instruments in the Lord's hands to accomplish His will. God is so completely just that He leaves no work done for His purposes unpaid.

When Egypt fell, God promised to make a horn sprout for Israel, which is a Bible picture of reviving power and hope. God would also open Ezekiel's mouth so the exiles would finally listen to his words as a true prophet. While worldly empires collapse, God preserves and strengthens His covenant people.

differ.view: The budding horn points ahead to the coming Messiah, Jesus Christ, who brings full strength and redemption to God's people.
The horn refers directly to the renewal of strength and encouragement for the Jewish people when God judged Egypt, rather than the Messiah.
